body:
What makes a period of hot weather a heatwave?

A heatwave is a period of unusually high temperature that meets the meteorological criteria used for the relevant location. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses both departure from the normal temperature and specified absolute maximum-temperature thresholds in its operational classification.

Ordinary summer heat and a formally classified heatwave are not identical. The same maximum temperature may represent a very unusual event at one location but be relatively close to normal at another.

IMD heatwave criteria

According to the criteria reproduced in IMD's 17 February 2026 National Weather Forecasting Centre press release, the following conditions apply.

Initial temperature conditions

  • For plains, the maximum temperature must reach at least 40°C.
  • For hilly regions, the maximum temperature must reach at least 30°C.

Classification based on departure from normal

  • Heatwave: Maximum temperature is 4.5°C to 6.4°C above normal.
  • Severe heatwave: Maximum temperature is at least 6.5°C above normal.

Classification based on actual maximum temperature (plains only)

  • Heatwave: Actual maximum temperature reaches 45°C or above.
  • Severe heatwave: Actual maximum temperature reaches 47°C or above.

For coastal stations, IMD gives a separate criterion: the maximum temperature must be at least 37°C and its departure from normal must be at least 4.5°C. For a heatwave declaration, the applicable criteria must be met at at least 2 stations in a meteorological subdivision for at least 2 consecutive days; declaration is made on the second day.

These are meteorological classification thresholds, not personal safety limits. Heat-related illness can occur below a formal heatwave threshold, especially during physical exertion, high humidity or prolonged exposure.

Why extreme heat affects the human body

The human body produces heat through metabolism and gains heat from its surroundings. It loses heat through mechanisms such as radiation, air movement and evaporation of sweat. When environmental heat and physical activity exceed the body's ability to lose heat, heat stress develops.

Humidity is important because sweat cools the body mainly when it evaporates. In humid air, evaporation becomes less effective. A hot, humid day can therefore produce serious physiological strain even if the measured air temperature is lower than on a very dry day.

Heat exposure may cause dehydration, cramps, dizziness, weakness and heat exhaustion. Severe overheating can progress to heatstroke, a medical emergency involving dangerous overheating and disturbance of normal brain function.

Why hot nights increase risk

When night-time temperatures remain high, people and buildings have less opportunity to cool after a hot day. Continued exposure can interfere with sleep and recovery, especially where houses have poor ventilation and residents lack access to cooling.

A hot night and an exceptionally high daytime maximum temperature are related heat hazards, but they measure different parts of the daily temperature cycle. Daytime heatwave classification should not be confused with a separate assessment of unusually warm nights.

Who is especially vulnerable?

Heat risk depends on both environmental conditions and individual circumstances. Groups that may face greater risk include:

  • Older adults, infants and young children.
  • Pregnant people and people with certain chronic illnesses.
  • People working outdoors or performing strenuous physical activity.
  • People living in crowded or poorly ventilated dwellings.
  • People with limited access to safe drinking water, shade, rest or cooling.

Outdoor workers may experience substantial heat exposure even where a weather station does not record the highest temperatures, because direct sunlight, reflected heat and physical exertion add to the burden on the body.

Reading a heatwave warning correctly

An IMD warning communicates anticipated meteorological danger over a specified area and period. The practical response should consider local conditions, health vulnerability and official public-health advice. The absence of a severe-heatwave classification does not mean that prolonged outdoor work is risk-free.

Prelims focus

  • IMD's initial maximum-temperature conditions are 40°C for plains and 30°C for hills.
  • A departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C above normal meets the heatwave departure criterion.
  • A departure of at least 6.5°C above normal meets the severe-heatwave departure criterion.
  • For plains, actual maximum temperatures of 45°C and 47°C are the respective heatwave and severe-heatwave thresholds.
  • High humidity reduces the cooling effectiveness of sweat evaporation.
  • Trap: Formal heatwave classification and the temperature at which an individual becomes ill are not the same thing.

[Sources: India Meteorological Department, National Weather Forecasting Centre, Definition/Criteria annex to press release dated 17 February 2026, Heat Wave criteria, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 7, Weather, Climate and Adaptations of Animals to Climate, printed pp. 68–72, 2018–19 reprint; National Centre for Disease Control, Public Health Advisory: Extreme Heat/Heatwave, 13 May 2026, sections on heat-related illnesses and danger signs, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: IMD heatwave criteria compare departure and actual-temperature methods after initial thresholds, with a separate coastal rule requiring both conditions.
pictures.caption: IMD uses both unusually high departures and actual maximum temperatures to classify heatwaves.

title: Heatwaves: IMD Thresholds, Heat Stress and Vulnerable Populations

body:
Why a heat action plan is necessary

A Heat Action Plan (HAP) is a coordinated public-health and disaster-preparedness approach for reducing illness and deaths during extreme heat. It connects weather warnings with actions by government departments, healthcare facilities, employers, communities and individuals.

A warning is useful only when the people exposed to danger understand it and can take appropriate action. A heat action plan therefore goes beyond forecasting: it identifies vulnerable groups, communicates precautions and prepares essential services.

The urban heat island effect

Built-up parts of a city can remain warmer than surrounding less-developed areas. This is called the urban heat island effect.

Several factors contribute to the effect:

  • Roads, roofs and other hard surfaces absorb and store solar heat.
  • Limited tree cover reduces shade and the cooling provided by vegetation.
  • Buildings may restrict air movement in densely developed streets.
  • Vehicles, air-conditioning equipment and other activities release additional heat.
  • Stored heat may be released after sunset, contributing to warmer nights.

The urban heat island effect is not the same as an officially declared heatwave. It is a local environmental condition that can increase exposure during normal hot weather and make a regional heatwave more dangerous.

Cooling measures for buildings and neighbourhoods

Cool roofs use surfaces that reflect more incoming sunlight or otherwise reduce heat absorption, helping lower roof and indoor heat gain under suitable conditions. Shade trees, parks, ventilated public spaces and accessible drinking-water points can also reduce heat exposure.

Cooling measures work at different scales. A reflective roof can help an individual building, whereas tree cover and shaded public spaces can improve conditions across a street or neighbourhood. These measures complement, rather than replace, early warnings and health protection.

Gujarat's Heat Action Plan experience

Ahmedabad introduced a comprehensive Heat Action Plan in 2013, following the serious heat conditions experienced in 2010. It is recognised as South Asia's first comprehensive city-level heat-health action plan. Its approach brought together early warnings, public communication, healthcare preparedness and practical heat-risk reduction.

The Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority also coordinates heat-related preparedness at the state level. For the 2025–26 planning period, GSDMA reported preparation of a State Heat Action Plan and updated district- and city-level plans for 33 districts and 8 municipal corporations. These numbers describe that stated planning period, not a permanent rule about how many plans must exist in later years.

Protecting people who work in the heat

Construction workers, road workers, agricultural labourers, street vendors and other outdoor workers may face direct sunlight, reflected heat and substantial physical exertion. Their risk is influenced by the duration of exposure, humidity, clothing, access to water and whether they are accustomed to the working conditions.

Basic precautions include:

  • Scheduling strenuous outdoor work during cooler parts of the day where practicable.
  • Providing accessible safe drinking water and opportunities for regular hydration.
  • Using shade or cooler resting places and allowing appropriate rest breaks.
  • Wearing suitable light, breathable clothing and protecting the head from direct sunlight.
  • Recognising early symptoms of heat illness and ensuring prompt access to help.

People with health conditions affecting their ability to tolerate heat may require additional precautions based on medical advice.

Heat exhaustion and heatstroke must be distinguished

ConditionTypical warning signsBasic response
Heat exhaustionWeakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, thirst and often heavy sweating.Move to a cool place, rest, cool the body and drink fluids if fully alert and able to swallow.
HeatstrokeSevere overheating with confusion, altered consciousness, collapse or seizures.Seek emergency medical help immediately and begin cooling while help is arranged.

Heatstroke is a medical emergency. Sweating may be present or absent, so absence of sweating is not required to suspect it. A person who is unconscious or unable to swallow safely should not be given drinks by mouth.

How a heat warning becomes protective action

IMD issues forecasts and weather warnings. State and local authorities, health departments, urban bodies and other responsible institutions communicate the risk and coordinate precautions. Healthcare services prepare for heat-related illnesses, while employers and community organisations help reduce exposure.

Clear messages should identify the expected danger, the period of risk, the groups needing extra care and the precautions people can take. Communication should reach people who may not regularly use smartphones or internet services.

Prelims focus

  • The urban heat island effect is associated with heat-storing surfaces, reduced vegetation and urban activity.
  • Ahmedabad introduced its comprehensive Heat Action Plan in 2013.
  • A Heat Action Plan links warnings, public communication, healthcare preparedness and exposure reduction.
  • Cool roofs and shade are heat-risk reduction measures.
  • Heatstroke with altered consciousness requires emergency medical assistance.
  • Trap: Urban heat islands and meteorological heatwaves are related but distinct concepts.

[Sources: National Centre for Disease Control, Climate Change and Health: Driving Local Action, November 2023, case study Heat Action Plan for Ahmedabad City, Gujarat: Development and Lessons, pp. 82–87; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Chapter XIII, section 13.8, Preparation and Updation of Disaster Management Plans, reported 2025–26 plan status, consulted 2 November 2026; National Centre for Disease Control, Public Health Advisory: Extreme Heat/Heatwave, 13 May 2026, and Strengthening Health Systems Preparedness for Heat Related Illnesses in India, 2023.]

pictures.alt: Road workers rest under a shaded canopy with drinking water beside a sunlit road in an Indian city on a hot afternoon.
pictures.caption: Shade, drinking water and rest help reduce heat exposure during outdoor work.

pictures.alt: IMD warnings guide state and local coordination of healthcare, employer and community actions to protect health; Ahmedabad introduced its plan in 2013.
pictures.caption: A heat action plan connects weather forecasts with communication, protection and healthcare readiness.

title: Heat Action Plans: Urban Heat, Occupational Exposure and Gujarat's Experience

body:
What is a cold wave?

A cold wave is a period of unusually low minimum temperature that meets the meteorological criteria used for the relevant location. It is not defined simply by whether a person feels cold.

Cold-wave risk depends on temperature, wind, exposure, shelter and individual vulnerability. People without adequate clothing or housing may suffer serious effects even when an official cold-wave criterion has not been met.

IMD cold-wave thresholds

According to the criteria reproduced in IMD's 17 February 2026 National Weather Forecasting Centre press release, classification uses the following conditions.

Initial temperature conditions

  • For plains, the minimum temperature must be 10°C or below.
  • For hilly regions, the minimum temperature must be 0°C or below.

Classification based on departure from normal

  • Cold wave: Minimum temperature is 4.5°C to 6.4°C below normal.
  • Severe cold wave: Minimum temperature is at least 6.5°C below normal.

Classification based on actual minimum temperature

For the plains, IMD also specifies absolute minimum-temperature criteria:

  • Cold wave: Minimum temperature is 4°C or below.
  • Severe cold wave: Minimum temperature is 2°C or below.

For coastal stations, the stated criterion requires a minimum-temperature departure of at least 4.5°C below normal together with an actual minimum temperature of 15°C or below. For a cold-wave declaration, the applicable criteria must be met at at least 2 stations in a meteorological subdivision for at least 2 consecutive days; declaration is made on the second day.

Cold wave versus cold day

A cold wave is principally classified using an abnormally low minimum temperature. A cold day is associated with an abnormally low maximum temperature, subject to the relevant minimum-temperature condition.

In the cited IMD criteria, a cold day requires a minimum temperature of 10°C or below in the plains or 0°C or below in the hills, along with a maximum temperature 4.5°C to 6.4°C below normal. A severe cold day has a maximum-temperature departure of at least 6.5°C below normal.

This distinction is important because a very cold night does not necessarily mean that the following day's maximum temperature will also be abnormally low.

How severe cold affects health

Low temperatures increase the body's loss of heat. Prolonged exposure can cause hypothermia, in which body temperature falls dangerously low. Warning signs may include intense shivering, unusual tiredness, confusion and reduced alertness. Very cold conditions may also aggravate some existing respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses.

Older adults, infants, people sleeping outdoors and those without sufficient warm clothing or shelter are especially vulnerable. Outdoor workers can also face prolonged exposure, particularly in windy or wet conditions.

Standard precautions during cold conditions

  • Wear suitable layers of warm, dry clothing and cover exposed parts of the body.
  • Keep living spaces adequately sheltered from cold while maintaining safe ventilation.
  • Pay special attention to older adults, infants and people without reliable shelter.
  • Avoid unnecessary prolonged exposure to very cold weather.
  • Do not use charcoal or other unvented fuel-burning heaters inside closed rooms because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.
  • Seek medical help for suspected hypothermia or a person who becomes confused or unusually drowsy after cold exposure.

Comparing flood, drought and temperature-related hazards

Floods, droughts, heatwaves and cold waves are connected to weather, but they differ in their primary observations, the speed at which damage may develop and the most useful public precautions.

Flood preparedness emphasises rainfall and river monitoring, safe land use, drainage and timely movement away from dangerous water. Drought preparedness emphasises monitoring water deficits over time, conserving supplies, protecting agriculture and supporting affected livelihoods. Heatwave preparedness emphasises early communication, reducing heat exposure, hydration and identifying heat illness. Cold-wave preparedness emphasises adequate shelter, safe warmth and protection of vulnerable people.

Common principles of effective preparedness

Despite these differences, the same basic risk-management principles apply. Hazards must be monitored, vulnerable people identified, official information communicated clearly and practical precautions taken before avoidable losses occur.

Reliable forecasts do not remove physical vulnerability. A warning about rising river water cannot protect a household unless its occupants know where to go. A drought assessment does not by itself provide drinking water. A heatwave alert cannot protect an outdoor worker who has no opportunity for shade or rest. Effective disaster management therefore combines hazard information with achievable protective action.

Prelims focus

  • Cold-wave criteria use minimum temperature and its departure from normal.
  • Cold-day criteria use unusually low maximum temperature with the specified minimum-temperature condition.
  • For plains, the cited IMD absolute minimum-temperature thresholds are 4°C for cold wave and 2°C for severe cold wave.
  • Hypothermia is a dangerous reduction in body temperature.
  • Flood risk reduction, drought planning and heat or cold protection require different practical measures.
  • Trap: A cold wave and a cold day are not interchangeable meteorological classifications.

[Sources: India Meteorological Department, National Weather Forecasting Centre, Definition/Criteria annex to press release dated 17 February 2026, Cold Wave and Cold Day criteria, consulted 2 November 2026; IMD, Cold Wave Frequently Asked Questions, sections on cold-wave classification and precautions, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2026–27, Chapter 6, pp. 60–66; National Centre for Disease Control, Public Health Advisory: Extreme Heat/Heatwave, 13 May 2026, consulted 2 November 2026.]
